title: Japan’s consumption tax cut would widen the fiscal deficit and push JGB yields higher
gist: Oxford Economics argues Japan's approved cut of the food consumption tax from 8% to 1% for FY2027-2028 cannot realistically be funded without debt, so it raises its 10-year JGB yield forecast to 3% by end-2026 (from 2.8%) and sees the primary balance stuck near a 3% of GDP deficit through 2028. The bond market has barely reacted so far; the repricing catalysts are the September tax policy outline and the December FY2027 budget process.

themes.theme: Food consumption tax cut and its funding gap

insights.claim: Japan's Takaichi government has approved cutting the food consumption tax to 1% from 8% for FY2027-2028 (Q2 2027-Q1 2029) with an explicit pledge not to fund it with debt.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: A concrete, dated fiscal loosening in Japan is now policy rather than campaign talk, so it belongs in 2027-2029 JGB supply and inflation assumptions.
insights.quote: Japan’s Takaichi government approved a plan to cut the food consumption tax to 1% from 8% without resorting to debt finance in FY2027-2028 (Q2 2027-Q1 2029).

insights.claim: Oxford Economics' modelling puts the annual revenue loss from Japan's food consumption tax cut at roughly JPY5trn.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: JPY5trn a year is the size of the hole markets must decide is filled by spending cuts or by extra JGB issuance.
insights.quote: Our modelling suggests that the tax cut will reduce annual tax revenue by around JPY5trn.

insights.claim: The no-debt-finance pledge attached to Japan's food consumption tax cut is not credible: roughly half of the JPY5trn annual revenue loss is assumed to end up debt-financed, with only the remainder covered by non-tax revenues and expenditure cuts.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Take the government's funding promise at a discount: an extra ~JPY2.5trn of annual borrowing is the working assumption for JGB supply.
insights.quote: Although some of the losses will be financed by non-tax revenues and cuts in expenses, we assume that half of the revenue loss will be financed by debt.

insights.claim: The core reason Japan's tax cut turns into wider deficits is simply that replacement revenue is hard to find, not that the government intends to borrow.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Watch the September revenue-offset details as the direct test of this mechanism; a credible offset package would invalidate the deficit and yield upgrades.

themes.theme: Primary balance path and the 2029 consolidation forcing function

insights.claim: Japan's primary balance is now forecast to deteriorate to and stay around a 3% of GDP deficit through 2027-2028 because of the food consumption tax cut.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: A structurally wider primary deficit is the fundamental justification for a higher JGB term premium and a weaker yen bias.
insights.quote: The primary balance will stay at around a 3% of GDP deficit in 2027-2028, before improving from 2029

insights.claim: Fiscal consolidation in Japan is expected to be imposed by the arithmetic of a rising debt-to-GDP ratio rather than chosen, with the turn arriving only from 2029 — after two full years of a wider deficit.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: The fiscal correction is back-loaded past 2028, so the near-term risk skew for JGBs is one-directional until the debt ratio itself forces a policy response.

themes.theme: JGB yield forecast upgrade and the repricing calendar

insights.claim: The 10-year Japanese government bond yield forecast has been raised to around 3% by the end of 2026, up from a prior 2.8% path, on the fiscal consequences of the consumption tax cut.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: A 20bp upgrade to the end-2026 10-year JGB forecast argues for staying short duration in JGBs and watching the knock-on for global term premia.
insights.quote: We now think the long-term JGB yield will rise to around 3% by the end of 2026, instead of staying at 2.8%.
insights.locator: We now think the long-term JGB yield

insights.claim: The JGB market has so far barely reacted to the approved food consumption tax cut, implying the fiscal deterioration is not yet in the price.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: Muted spot reaction plus a forecast upgrade is the setup for an asymmetric short-duration or steepener trade before the market catches up.
insights.quote: While the bond market’s reaction to the news has been limited so far, we think the market will start to price in the fiscal effects of the coming tax cut

insights.claim: Two specific dated catalysts are identified for the JGB repricing: the tax policy outline in September and the FY2027 budget process in December, when revenue-offset details become available.
insights.speaker: Yasuko Koido
insights.so_what: These are the event dates to position around rather than trading the headline approval itself.
